analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for police to use excessive force, steal property, or destroy recordings of their own misconduct.
analysis.headline: Senator Booker introduced the bill in February 2026 with no cosponsors, and the Senate sent it to the Judiciary Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates new federal crimes for people acting with government authority. It would let federal prosecutors charge officers who cause bodily injury using excessive force, who steal money, property, or drugs from people they search or arrest, or who destroy or block recordings of police activity. Penalties run up to 30 years for offenses involving death, and there would be no time limit to prosecute cases where someone died.
analysis.who_benefits: People subjected to excessive force by officers, people from whom officers steal during searches or arrests, people in jails and prisons, and bystanders who film police activity. Federal prosecutors and the Justice Department would gain new charging tools for police misconduct.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal crime of causing bodily injury by intentionally using excessive force, punishable by up to 10 years, or up to 30 years when the offense involves kidnapping, an attempt to kill, or death [S2].
Makes it a federal crime for officers to steal money, property worth more than $25, or drugs from people in their custody or from homes and vehicles they search, with penalties up to 10 years [S2].

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 20 years, to destroy recordings of police activity, use force to stop someone from lawfully filming police, or destroy other evidence of a color-of-law violation [S2].
Allows prosecution with no statute of limitations for offenses under the bill that result in death, and a 7-year limit for other offenses [S2].
Criminalizes failing to intervene: an officer with the duty, opportunity, and ability to stop known excessive force who deliberately does not faces the same penalties as the officer who used it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and agencies, which would face new federal criminal exposure for conduct currently handled mainly through state prosecution, internal discipline, or civil suits, and the Justice Department, which would bear the cost of investigating and prosecuting these cases.

drawbacks.text: The federal government already has a criminal civil-rights statute (18 U.S.C. 242) covering misconduct under color of law; critics argue overlapping federal crimes add a second layer of prosecution on top of state law without addressing civil remedies like qualified immunity, the barrier that most often blocks victims' lawsuits [S2].

The definitions are broad: force is criminal when an officer 'consciously disregards a substantial risk' it is excessive, and theft covers property over $25, which supporters of police argue could chill officers making split-second decisions and pull more routine misconduct cases into federal court [S2].

Even if enacted, enforcement depends entirely on federal prosecutors choosing to bring cases, which has historically been rare against officers; a statute alone does not guarantee accountability [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give federal prosecutors real criminal tools against excessive force, officer theft, and destruction of recordings, which would matter most to people in heavily policed communities and to detainees. The costs fall on officers facing new federal exposure and on prosecutors' resources, and the bill leaves civil barriers like qualified immunity untouched, so its real-world effect would depend heavily on how willingly Justice Department officials use it.

outcome.mechanism: Booker introduced the bill and the Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where it sits with zero cosponsors and no scheduled action.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Under Color of Law Accountability Act in the Senate on February 9, 2026 [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, its only action so far [S4].
No senator has cosponsored the bill [S3].

The bill would create a new chapter of federal criminal law covering excessive force, theft by officers, obstruction of recordings of police activity, failure to intervene, and evidence destruction, with penalties up to 30 years [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet, in either direction. The bill has not advanced, so officers and agencies remain under the current rules, and people harmed by police misconduct have gained nothing new.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is a Democrat's solo effort with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan line has formed yet; the Republican-majority Judiciary Committee has taken no action on it.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill exposes individual officers to new federal felony charges and up to 30-year sentences for excessive force, theft, destroying recordings, or failing to stop known misconduct. Police organizations have generally opposed expanding federal criminal liability for officers, and an officer's gain from the bill dying is the public's loss of a new accountability tool.

The theft provision explicitly applies to people in custody of correctional facilities 'whether run by a government agency or private entity,' so staff at private facilities would face the same federal theft charges. People in those facilities, who are often victimized with little recourse, would gain a federal remedy.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and a 55-seat Republican Senate majority, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote this Congress; most solo criminal-justice bills at this stage die quietly in committee at the end of the session.
